Title: Major decline in maternal and child deaths worldwide
NewsSummary: Child deaths have been cut nearly in half since 1990, and maternal deaths by almost a quarter. The pace accelerated after Millennium Development Goals were set, yet few countries are on track to meet ambitious targets.

content.text: Child deaths have been cut nearly in half since 1990, and maternal deaths by almost a quarter. The pace accelerated after Millennium Development Goals were set, yet few countries are on track to meet ambitious targets.

These results appeared in two separate studies Global, regional, and national levels of neonatal, infant, and  under-5 mortality during 1990-2013 and Global, regional, and national levels and causes of maternal mortality during 1990-2013 published in The Lancet. The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington spearheaded the work, with Dr Zulfiqar Bhutta, Founding Director of the Centre for Excellence in Women and Child Health at Aga Khan University as one of the authors.

In 2000, the Millennium Development Goals were established by the United Nations to drive maternal and child deaths down by 2015. Child and maternal deaths had been falling in most countries since the 1980s, but the pace accelerated after the goals were set.
Researchers believe that if this trend continues, child deaths will fall from more than six million in 2013 to fewer than four million in 2030.

The leading cause of maternal death globally is medical complications during childbirth and in the period post-delivery. Globally, approximately one-quarter of maternal deaths were found to occur during childbirth and in the following 24 hours. Another quarter happen during pregnancy, and the remaining deaths occur up to one year after delivery.

The study suggests that key drivers of progress in reducing child deaths at the global level include maternal education, medical and public health innovations, and rising income. For each additional year of school mothers complete, child deaths drop by more than eight per cent.
Child survival - MDG 4 - regional and country findings:
*    Forty-five countries, including 27 in the developing world, are on track to meet the MDG 4 target of reducing child death rates by two-thirds of 1990 levels by 2015.
*    Two-thirds of the global decline in child deaths since 2000 occurred in just nine countries - India, China, Ethiopia, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Pakistan, Brazil, Afghanistan, and Nigeria.
*    The 10 countries with the lowest child survival rates in 2013 were all in sub-Saharan Africa including Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
Maternal survival - MDG 5 - regional and country findings:

*    Maternal mortality in sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean either held steady or increased from 1990 to the mid-2000s - even doubling in Southern Africa - before beginning a fast decline following establishment of the MDGs.
*    The United States was among just eight countries that experienced an increase in maternal death rates since 2003 - joining countries including Afghanistan and El Salvador.
*    Sixteen countries - most in Central and Eastern Europe - are likely to achieve the MDG 5 target of a 75 per cent reduction in their 1990 maternal death rate by 2015.
